Cosy analysis

Louise Bernard

2024-03-18

Introduction

This document presents the results of the impact of the adoption of cosy tariff on smart meter electricity consumption at the household level.

In summary, switching to the Cosy rate appears to effectively encourage customers to increase their electricity consumption during incentivised periods (cosy morning and afternoon) while decreasing usage during peak and other times, with an overall slight increase in daily consumption.

Difference in differences

We run the following model by period and on total daily consumption for all customers that have adopted Cosy in the past year:

\[Consumption_{it} = \alpha OnCosy_{it} + \delta_t + \gamma_i + GSP \times \delta_t+ \epsilon_{it} \] with:

  • \(Consumption_{it}\) - electricty consumption in kWh (Table 1) and as share of daily consumption (Table 2) for customer \(i\) on day \(t\)
  • \(OnCosy_{it}\) a dummy variable equals 1 if the customer has switched to Cosy, 0 otherwise 1
  • \(\delta_t\), \(\gamma_i\), $ GSP _t$ are day \(t\), customer \(i\), and GSP regions times day fixed effects The standard errors are clustered at the customer (MPAN) level.

Consumption by period

This table presents the effects of switching to the “Cosy” rate on customers’ electricity consumption across different times of the day using consumption in kilowatt-hours (kWh) per period, along with a separate analysis for overall daily consumption. Here’s a summary of the findings:

  • Afternoon Cosy (Model 1): Customers on the Cosy rate increased their electricity consumption by an average of 1.770 kWh during the afternoon cosy period.
  • Morning Cosy (Model 2): There was an even larger increase in consumption during the morning cosy period, with customers consuming an additional 3.079 kWh on average.
  • Other Time (Model 3): Conversely, consumption during other times of the day not specified as cosy morning or afternoon decreased by 2.664 kWh.
  • Peak Rate (Model 4): Consumption during peak rate times decreased by 1.204 kWh, showing that customers are reducing their usage during more expensive or high-demand periods.
  • Overall Daily Consumption (Model 5): Despite these shifts in consumption patterns throughout the day, the overall daily consumption increased slightly by 1.073 kWh, suggesting that while there’s a redistribution of when electricity is used, the total daily usage still went up on the Cosy rate.

All of these coefficients are statistically significant at the 1 percent significance level.

In summary, switching to the Cosy rate appears to effectively encourage customers to increase their electricity consumption during incentivised periods (cosy morning and afternoon) while decreasing usage during peak and other times, with an overall slight increase in daily consumption.

Share electricity consumption

The table’s analysis shows how adopting the Cosy rate plan impacts customers’ electricity usage patterns across different times of the day, focusing on the change in the share of daily electricity consumption per period.

  • Afternoon Cosy Period: After switching to the Cosy rate, the proportion of electricity used during the afternoon cosy period increased by 6.62 percentage points. This indicates customers are more inclined to consume electricity during these hours under the Cosy rate.

  • Morning Cosy Period: The adoption of the Cosy rate led to an even more pronounced increase in electricity use during the morning cosy period, with a 12.56 percentage point rise in its share of daily consumption. This suggests a significant behavioral shift towards consuming more electricity in the morning hours.

  • Other Times: Contrarily, there’s a decrease in the share of electricity consumption during times not designated as cosy by 14.71 percentage points, reflecting a shift away from electricity usage during these periods.

  • Peak Rate Times: The share of daily electricity usage during peak rate times also saw a decrease, falling by 4.75 percentage points. This reduction implies that consumers are adjusting their usage to avoid higher-cost periods.

Event study

We run the following model by period for all customers that have adopted Cosy in the past year:

\[Consumption_{it} = \sum^W _{w={-52, -9, ..., 1, ..,52}} \alpha_w WeeksSinceCosy^w_{it} + X\beta + \delta_t + \gamma_i + \epsilon_{it} \] where: - \(WeeksSinceCosy^w_{it}\) is a categorical variable equals to the number of weeks before and after the adoption of Cosy. We use the week prior adoption as omitted category.

Consumption by period

The charts show the event study coefficients for each specified period. We find that coefficients are consistent with those from the difference-in-differences analysis.

Interestingly, the trend for the Morning Cosy period doesn’t appear to be as stable, almost indicating an overall decrease in consumption over time, with still a noticeable jump at the point of adoption. This pattern suggests that the interaction between time trends and the effects of the treatment might be more pronounced during the Morning Cosy period than in other periods or something as the unbalanced panel data.

Similarly, the coefficients on Afternoon Cosy pre -adoption are consistently negative - I think we could improve this part of the analysis.

Callaway Sant’Anna DiD

This estimator refines traditional DiD analyses by offering more robust handling of heterogeneous treatment effects over time. The data aggregation at the week level necessitates adjustment (division by 7) for direct comparison with previous estimations, which were at a daily granularity. This aggregation may smooth out some of the daily volatility but still captures broader trends.

Key Components Analyzed

Overall ATT (Average Treatment Effect on the Treated)

This measures the average impact of the Cosy rate on all treated customers.

To compare the recently calculated daily coefficients with the previous coefficients provided, let’s line them up:

Previous Coefficients (per period):

  • Afternoon Cosy: +1.770 kWh
  • Morning Cosy: +3.079 kWh
  • Other: -2.664 kWh
  • Peak Rate: -1.204 kWh
  • Overall: +1.073 kWh (Overall daily consumption increase)

Recently Calculated Daily Coefficients:

  • Afternoon Cosy: +2.33 kWh/day
  • Morning Cosy: +3.41 kWh/day
  • Other: -2.61 kWh/day
  • Peak Rate: -1.34 kWh/day
  • Overall: +1.79 kWh/day

The comparison shows that the Callaway and Sant’Anna coefficients generally indicate a stronger effect of the Cosy rate on altering electricity consumption patterns across different periods compared to the initial coefficients provided. This includes larger increases in consumption during cosy periods and a slightly greater overall daily consumption increase.

Dynamic ATT

Similar to the event study approach, dynamic ATT analyzes how the treatment effect changes over time, offering insights into whether the impact of Cosy grows stronger, weaker, or remains consistent in the weeks following adoption. This can help identify any adaptation period or delayed effects.

Group ATT

This looks at the treatment effect within early to later adopters. It’s crucial for understanding if early adopters differed from later adopters.

Calendar ATT

This variation focuses on the treatment effect relative to the calendar time. Unsurprisingly, It shows that the effect of cosy are concentrated during autumn and winter seasons.
